unit.name: Structures and Earth Dynamics
unit.subtitle: Read folds, faults and unconformities, and link them to the rock cycle and plate tectonics

lessons.title: Folding and Tectonic Stress
lessons.description: How compressional stress buckles rock layers into folds, anticlines and synclines.
lessons.content_html:
Why Do Rocks Bend?

Rocks deep in the Earth behave very differently from rocks at the surface. Under extreme tectonic stress, buried rocks can slowly bend rather than break — a process that produces the folded landscapes geologists map today. Understanding folds is essential for reading geological maps and cross-sections in your exam.

When two tectonic plates converge, their edges are squeezed together. This compressional stress acts like a vice on the rock layers caught between the plates. The layers shorten horizontally and thicken vertically, producing folds that can range from gentle, barely perceptible warps to dramatic upright mountains of contorted strata.

Key Fact

Folds form when compressional stress shortens and thickens the crust. They are the signature structure of convergent plate boundaries and collision zones such as the Himalayas.

From Flat Beds to Folded Beds

Sedimentary rocks are originally deposited in roughly horizontal layers called strata. When stress is applied, those horizontal beds first tilt — they become dipping beds that slope at an angle to the horizontal. If stress continues, the dipping beds arch upward or downward into folds.

A fold that arches upward, with older rocks in the core, is called an antiform. The mirror image — a fold that sags downward, with younger rocks in the core — is a synform. In textbooks you will also see these called anticlines and synclines when geologists know which beds are older; for your exam, antiform and synform are the precise terms for geometry alone.

Each fold has two sloping sides called limbs. The imaginary plane that divides the fold symmetrically down its middle is the axial plane. Where the axial plane intersects the ground surface it leaves a trace on a geological map known as the axial plane trace. Identifying an axial plane trace on a map tells you where the crest or trough of a fold runs across the landscape.

Imagine a geological map showing three rock units: an older shale in the centre, flanked symmetrically by a younger limestone on each side, which is in turn flanked by an even younger sandstone. The pattern of older rock in the centre, with progressively younger rocks on both sides, is the map signature of an antiform. The axial plane trace runs along the line of oldest rock.

Now reverse the pattern: youngest rock in the centre, flanked by older units on each side. This is a synform. On a cross-section drawn perpendicular to the axial plane trace, the strata would curve downward like a bowl. Your textbook cross-sections will show these mirror-image curves clearly — use them alongside the map view to build a 3D picture of the fold.

Measuring Strike and Dip in the Field

To describe the orientation of a tilted rock surface, geologists measure two angles. Strike is the compass direction of a horizontal line on the dipping surface — think of it as the direction the bed runs across the landscape. Dip is the angle of maximum slope, measured downhill perpendicular to strike. A bed might strike north–south and dip 30° to the east, for example.

Both measurements are taken using a compass clinometer — an instrument that combines a magnetic compass for strike direction with a clinometer pendulum for dip angle. On a geological map, dip is shown by a small T-shaped symbol: the long bar lies along the strike direction and the short tick points in the dip direction, with the dip angle written alongside.

Key Fact

Dip and strike are complementary: strike runs along the bed, dip descends at right angles to it. The two measurements together fully describe the orientation of any planar rock surface in three dimensions.

Geologists measure dip and strike at natural outcrops — cliff faces, stream banks, road cuttings, and quarry walls. Safety precautions at field exposures include: staying away from undercut cliff faces, wearing a hard hat where rockfall is possible, not hammering rock without eye protection, and never working at the base of an unstable face. Your school will follow a site-specific risk assessment for any fieldwork visit.

When using a compass clinometer, metal objects (including belt buckles and boots with steel toecaps) can deflect the magnetic needle. Hold the instrument well away from any metal before taking a bearing. Record each measurement in a field notebook immediately — memory fades quickly in windy or cold conditions.

Folds in the Wider Rock Record

Fold structures preserve the rock record over enormous timescales. In the UK, the Caledonian mountain-building event — caused by the collision of ancient plates during the Silurian and Devonian periods — produced the folded and faulted rocks now exposed in the Scottish Highlands and parts of Wales. The gentle folds of the Weald in southern England formed much later, during the Alpine compression that also built the Alps. Both sets of folds are visible at the surface today only because millions of years of erosion have stripped away the overlying rock, exposing the cores and limbs of ancient structures.

This lesson sets the scene for the rest of the unit. In the next lesson you will study faults — the structures that form when rocks break rather than bend under tectonic stress. Together, folds and faults are the two fundamental responses of rock to the forces operating at plate boundaries.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on folding often include a cross-section or map pattern. If asked to identify a fold type, look at which age rocks sit in the centre: oldest in the middle means antiform; youngest in the middle means synform. For a describe question, state the direction of closure (upward or downward), mention the limbs, and give the axial plane trace position. Never confuse dip (angle) with strike (compass direction) — examiners report this as a common error. Show all working when calculating dip angles from a scaled diagram.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Compressional stress at convergent plate boundaries shortens and thickens the crust, bending originally horizontal strata into folds.
  • An antiform arches upward with older rocks at its core; a synform sags downward with younger rocks at its core. Limbs are the sloping sides; the axial plane trace marks the crest or trough on a map.
  • Strike (compass direction along the bed) and dip (angle of maximum slope) are measured in the field with a compass clinometer and recorded on geological maps using the standard T-shaped symbol.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of measuring dip and strike to interpret geological structures in the field. In your answer, consider both the advantages and limitations of the method.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains clearly that dip and strike together define the 3D orientation of a bed; links to construction of cross-sections and geological maps; evaluates limitations (single measurement may not represent the whole limb; curved fold limbs give varying dip; magnetic anomalies can deflect compass; human error in reading clinometer). Reaches a balanced conclusion about the method's usefulness.
Secure: Explains what dip and strike mean and why both are needed; identifies at least one strength and one limitation; some attempt at conclusion.
Developing: Describes dip or strike correctly; identifies one advantage or one limitation; limited evaluation.
Emerging: Shows partial understanding of at least one term; little or no evaluation.

lessons.title: Faults and Fault Displacement
lessons.description: Recognise normal, reverse, thrust and strike-slip faults from the stresses that produce them.
lessons.content_html:
When Rocks Break Instead of Bend

In the previous lesson you saw that compressional stress can slowly bend buried rocks into folds. But rocks do not always bend — sometimes they fracture. A fault is a planar fracture along which measurable displacement has occurred. The type of fault that forms depends on the direction and nature of the stress applied to the rock.

Geologists classify faults by comparing the movement of two key blocks: the hanging wall and the footwall. Imagine standing on the fault plane itself — the block above you is the hanging wall, the block beneath your feet is the footwall. Whether the hanging wall moves up or down relative to the footwall tells you immediately which type of fault you are looking at.

Key Fact

There are four main fault types on the specification: normal, reverse, thrust, and strike-slip. Each is the product of a different type of tectonic stress — tensional, compressional, or shear.

Normal Faults — Tensional Stress

A normal fault forms when tensional stress pulls the crust apart. The hanging wall slides down relative to the footwall. Normal faults are the signature structure of divergent plate boundaries, where two plates move apart. The East African Rift Valley is a classic modern example: as the African plate is pulled apart by tensional stress, a central block drops down between parallel normal faults to form a rift valley. Fault planes in normal faults are typically steep, dipping at 60° or more.

On a geological map, you can recognise a normal fault by the displacement of rock units. A distinctive feature is that the rock sequence is repeated on either side of the fault — looking across the fault, each rock unit appears to continue but at a lower level on the downthrown side. In cross-section, the hanging wall drops, widening the exposure of younger surface rocks in the centre of a downfaulted block.

Reverse and Thrust Faults — Compressional Stress

A reverse fault forms when compressional stress drives the hanging wall upward relative to the footwall. This is the opposite of a normal fault. Reverse faults have steep fault planes, typically dipping at 45° or more.

When the fault plane is very shallow — dipping at less than 30° — the structure is specifically called a thrust fault. Thrust faults are spectacular: compressional stress can push entire sheets of older rock many kilometres over younger rocks. The Moine Thrust in north-west Scotland is a famous example, where ancient Precambrian rocks were thrust horizontally over younger Cambrian strata during the Caledonian orogeny. The diagnostic field observation is finding older rocks sitting directly on top of younger ones — apparently the “wrong way round” by the law of superposition.

Examiner reports consistently flag this mix-up. The key is the word “normal” — it refers to what happens normally under gravity: the hanging wall slips down. A reverse fault is the reverse of that — the hanging wall moves up. In a diagram, check: if the rocks on the left side of the fault appear to have moved upward, the left block is the hanging wall and it has gone up — reverse fault. If it has gone down — normal fault. Practise sketching both types with arrows showing the hanging-wall movement direction.

Strike-Slip Faults — Shear Stress

A strike-slip fault forms when shear stress causes the two sides of a fault to slide horizontally past each other. There is little or no vertical movement. Strike-slip faults are associated with conservative plate boundaries, where two plates grind sideways past each other. The San Andreas Fault in California is the world’s most studied strike-slip fault: the Pacific Plate moves north-west past the North American Plate at roughly 5–6 cm per year.

On a geological map, strike-slip faults are identified by the sideways offset of rock units, dykes, or other linear features that cross the fault. If you face the fault and the block on the other side has moved to the right, it is called a dextral (right-lateral) fault. If it has moved to the left, it is sinistral (left-lateral). Identifying the offset of a distinctive marker — such as a dyke displaced by a fault — is a common exam question on the practical-skills component.

Key Fact

Normal fault → tensional stress, hanging wall down (divergent boundaries). Reverse/thrust fault → compressional stress, hanging wall up (convergent boundaries). Strike-slip fault → shear stress, horizontal movement (conservative boundaries).

When a fault cuts across a series of rock units on a map, the units appear displaced — they start on one side of the fault line and continue at a different position on the other. For a normal or reverse fault, the displacement is vertical: units on the downthrown side are lower. For a strike-slip fault, units are shifted sideways. The amount of shift is called the fault displacement. You can calculate horizontal displacement by measuring the offset of a marker horizon on the map and applying the map scale. Always include units (metres or kilometres) in your answer.

Faults and Earthquakes

Faults are geologically active as long as the stress driving them continues. Movement is rarely smooth — blocks lock together until stress overcomes friction, then slip rapidly, releasing energy as seismic waves. This is the mechanism of most earthquakes. The zone of crushed and ground-up rock along the fault plane is called fault breccia. Deep faults that cut right through the lithosphere are particularly significant because they control the location of volcanic activity and earthquake zones, both of which you will meet in the plate boundaries lesson.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark compare question on faults, you must mention both features in each comparison — not just describe one fault. For example: “In a normal fault the hanging wall moves downward, whereas in a reverse fault the hanging wall moves upward.” Missing the comparison word (whereas/while/by contrast) is the most common reason students score 2 out of 4. For map questions, trace the displacement of a named rock unit or dyke across the fault line to justify your identification.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Faults are fractures in rock along which displacement has occurred. The hanging wall is above the fault plane; the footwall is below.
  • Normal faults (hanging wall down, tensional stress) form at divergent boundaries; reverse and thrust faults (hanging wall up, compressional stress) at convergent boundaries; strike-slip faults (horizontal movement, shear stress) at conservative boundaries.
  • Fault type is identified from the direction of displacement, the stress context, and map evidence such as the offset of rock units or dykes.

lessons.title: Unconformities and Reading 3D Structures
lessons.description: Angular unconformities mark gaps in the rock record — learn to read them and use strike-and-dip in 3D.
lessons.content_html:
Gaps Hidden in the Rock Record

The geological record is not a complete archive. Periods of erosion, non-deposition, and tectonic upheaval all leave gaps — intervals of time for which no rock survives at a given location. Geologists call these gaps unconformities. Recognising an unconformity in the field or on a map is one of the most powerful skills in stratigraphy, because the gap itself tells a story about ancient tectonic events.

The most visually striking type is the angular unconformity. In an angular unconformity, the beds below the erosion surface are tilted or folded at an angle to the beds above. The two sets of beds are not parallel. This angular discordance is immediately obvious in a cliff section or road cutting, and it records a specific sequence of geological events.

Key Fact

An angular unconformity is produced by four sequential events: (1) deposition of the lower beds, (2) deformation and tilting of those beds by tectonic stress, (3) uplift and erosion of the tilted surface, (4) subsidence and renewed deposition of horizontal beds on top of the eroded surface.

Reading the Four Stages

Stage 1 is straightforward: a sequence of sedimentary layers is deposited in a marine or fluvial environment, building up a stack of horizontal strata following the principle of original horizontality.

Stage 2 involves deformation. Tectonic forces fold or tilt the original beds, rotating them away from horizontal. This may happen during a mountain-building episode at a convergent plate boundary. The tilted strata are now exposed at the surface.

Stage 3 is erosion. As the rocks are uplifted, rivers, waves, and weathering strip away the tops of the tilted beds. This creates a flat erosion surface — the unconformity plane itself — that cuts across the tilted beds at an angle. Any rock originally above this surface is lost from the record: this is the gap.

Stage 4 is renewed deposition. The landscape subsides or sea level rises, and a new layer of sediment is deposited on top of the eroded surface. These new beds are horizontal (or gently dipping), discordant with the tilted beds below. The contact between the two sets of beds is the angular unconformity surface.

One of geology’s most celebrated outcrops is Siccar Point on the Berwickshire coast of Scotland. Here, near-vertical Silurian greywacke beds (around 435 million years old) are unconformably overlain by gently dipping Devonian red sandstone (around 370 million years old). The nearly 65-million-year gap in the record convinced James Hutton in 1788 that the Earth must be immeasurably old — far older than any biblical timescale suggested. This insight was a founding moment for modern geology and the concept of deep time.

When identifying this unconformity type in a cross-section, look for: (a) beds below the unconformity that dip at a steeper or different angle to those above, (b) a sharp erosion surface between them, and (c) a possible basal conglomerate just above the unconformity surface, formed from the eroded material of the older beds.

Reading Strike-and-Dip on a Geological Map

A geological map is a 2D representation of a 3D world. To reconstruct that third dimension, geologists use strike-and-dip data marked on the map at measured outcrops. Each symbol — a T-shape with a tick and a dip angle number — tells you the orientation of the bed at that exact point.

From several strike-and-dip measurements in an area you can begin to build a 3D picture. If all nearby dip arrows point in the same direction and at similar angles, the beds are simply tilted. If the arrows converge toward a line, that line is the hinge of a fold — an antiform if the beds dip away from it on both sides, a synform if they dip toward it. Strike-and-dip measurements also let you draw an accurate cross-section through the geology.

Key Fact

On a geological map, dip arrows pointing in the same direction indicate simply tilted beds. Dip arrows pointing toward each other from both sides indicate a synform; pointing away from each other indicate an antiform.

Using Six-Figure Grid References

To locate a specific outcrop or structural measurement precisely on a map, geologists use six-figure grid references. The first three digits give the easting (distance east of the grid origin) and the last three give the northing (distance north). On a geological map, structural measurements, fossil localities, and rock unit boundaries are all pinpointed this way. In your exam, the practical-skills component may ask you to read off or plot a grid reference from the simplified geological map provided.

To draw a cross-section: (1) Draw a straight line across the map along the section line. (2) Mark where each rock unit boundary crosses the line. (3) Read the dip angle and direction at the nearest strike-and-dip symbol for each unit. (4) Project each boundary down into the cross-section at the measured dip angle. (5) Connect the projected boundaries for each unit to show the underground geometry. An angular unconformity will appear as an angular break between the lower, tilted boundaries and the upper, more horizontal ones.

A cross-section in your textbook or on the the practical-skills component map will show these relationships. Study the cross-section alongside the map: the 2D map pattern of rock unit boundaries is the surface expression of the 3D geometry shown in the cross-section. Practise moving between both views until you can visualise the structure confidently.

Linking Unconformities to Earth History

An angular unconformity is more than a gap — it is a diary entry recording a cycle of mountain-building and erosion. The thickness of the missing record (the time gap) can be estimated by comparing the ages of the youngest bed below the unconformity and the oldest bed above it. In Britain, many major unconformities correspond to ancient orogenies: the Caledonian orogeny in the Silurian–Devonian, and the Variscan orogeny in the Carboniferous–Permian. Each left a surface of erosion that now separates rock sequences of very different structural style.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For sequence geological events questions involving an unconformity, work systematically from oldest to youngest using superposition and cross-cutting relationships: older tilted beds → deformation → erosion (the unconformity surface) → renewed deposition of upper beds. State each stage as a separate step. Do not confuse an angular unconformity (tilted below, horizontal above) with a disconformity (parallel beds with a gap). When drawing or labelling a cross-section, clearly mark the unconformity surface and annotate which beds are older and younger.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • An angular unconformity is a surface of erosion separating tilted lower beds from horizontal upper beds, recording four stages: deposition, deformation, erosion, and renewed deposition.
  • Strike-and-dip symbols on a geological map describe the 3D orientation of rock surfaces; multiple symbols allow you to identify tilted beds, antiforms, and synforms, and to construct accurate cross-sections.
  • Six-figure grid references locate structural measurements precisely on a map, allowing features to be communicated unambiguously between geologists.

lessons.title: The Rock Cycle
lessons.description: How igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic processes link over geological time, and the rates at which they operate.
lessons.content_html:
Connecting the Three Rock Types

In the earlier units you studied igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks as separate categories. The rock cycle shows how all three types are connected — each can be transformed into another given enough time and the right conditions of temperature, pressure, erosion, or burial. No rock is permanent; every rock is on a journey.

The driving forces of the rock cycle are two distinct sources of energy. Heat from the Earth’s interior (geothermal energy) drives igneous and metamorphic processes: it melts rock to form magma, powers volcanic activity, and provides the high temperatures needed for metamorphism. Energy from the Sun drives the surface processes: it heats the atmosphere, drives weather and river systems, and therefore controls erosion, transport, and deposition of sediment. Understanding this energy framework prevents the common misconception that the rock cycle has a single driver or a single pathway.

Key Fact

The rock cycle has two energy sources: geothermal energy from the Earth’s interior (driving igneous activity and metamorphism) and solar energy at the surface (driving weathering, erosion, and deposition).

The Main Pathways

There is no single fixed pathway through the rock cycle — a rock can take many routes depending on what happens to it next. However, some common journeys are worth understanding. An igneous rock at the surface is immediately attacked by weathering and erosion. The fragments (clasts) are transported by rivers, wind, or ice, then deposited as sediment. With burial, compaction, and cementation, the sediment lithifies into sedimentary rock.

If that sedimentary rock is buried more deeply and exposed to elevated temperatures and pressures — but not melted — it recrystallises in the solid state to form metamorphic rock. This distinction matters: metamorphism is solid-state change. If melting occurs, the process becomes igneous, not metamorphic. If the metamorphic rock is buried even further and melts completely, it forms magma, which can cool underground as an intrusive igneous rock or erupt as lava to form an extrusive igneous rock — completing one loop of the cycle.

Critically, shortcuts exist. A sedimentary rock at the surface can be eroded back to sediment without ever becoming metamorphic. A metamorphic rock exposed at the surface by uplift and erosion can be directly weathered. The cycle has many parallel loops running simultaneously, and they operate at vastly different rates.

Most rock-cycle processes operate on timescales of millions of years — this is the principle of gradualism (also called uniformitarianism). River erosion, sediment deposition, burial, and metamorphism all operate gradually. However, geology also recognises catastrophism — the view that some major events happen suddenly and dramatically.

The end-Cretaceous meteorite impact is the classic example. Around 66 million years ago, a bolide roughly 10 km across struck the Yucatán Peninsula. The impact triggered wildfires, tsunamis, and a prolonged “impact winter” caused by dust and debris blocking sunlight. The result was mass extinction, including the non-avian dinosaurs. This single catastrophic event left a clear geological signature — an iridium-rich layer at the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary that is found worldwide. Modern geology accepts that both gradualism and catastrophism are real: most processes are gradual, but rare catastrophic events can punctuate the record.

The Rate Problem

Different parts of the rock cycle operate at very different speeds. River erosion can cut a gorge metres deep in a human lifetime. In contrast, the subduction of oceanic crust back into the mantle — completing the plate-tectonic loop of the rock cycle — takes tens of millions of years. Metamorphism in a subduction zone happens over millions of years as rocks are slowly dragged to depth. Understanding this rate difference is important for interpreting the rock record: a thin sedimentary layer might represent a very short, high-energy event (a storm deposit, for example), while a thick sequence of deep-sea mudstone represents millions of years of quiet, slow accumulation.

Key Fact

Geological processes span an enormous range of rates — from volcanic eruptions lasting hours or days, to the subduction cycle operating over tens of millions of years. The rock cycle therefore operates simultaneously on human timescales (eruptions, floods) and deep-time timescales (mountain building, ocean floor renewal).

A common mistake is to treat the rock cycle as a one-way conveyor belt: igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → back to igneous. This is only one of many possible pathways. Any rock type can be eroded to sediment, any rock type can be metamorphosed, and any rock type can eventually melt to produce a new magma. The power of the rock cycle model is precisely that it is cyclic and multi-directional. When answering exam questions, avoid writing “sedimentary rocks become metamorphic rocks” without adding “…if buried and subjected to elevated temperature and pressure” — the condition matters.

Deep Time and the Rock Cycle

The rock cycle can only be appreciated against the backdrop of geological time. The Earth is approximately 4.6 billion years old. The oldest known rocks on Earth (the Acasta Gneiss of Canada) are around 4 billion years old, yet even these have been metamorphosed and deformed many times since their formation. The constant recycling of crustal material means that almost no original Hadean crust survives. The rock cycle, driven by plate tectonics and solar energy, has been continuously reworking the Earth’s surface for as long as the planet has existed.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Rock cycle questions often use command words like explain or evaluate rather than just describe. When you explain a pathway, you must name the process that transforms one rock type into another (e.g. “burial and compaction converts sediment into sedimentary rock”) — just naming the rock types without the process will not earn marks. For extended response questions on catastrophism vs gradualism, give a specific example of each (e.g. meteorite impact for catastrophism, river erosion for gradualism) and reach a conclusion about which view is more applicable to most of the rock record.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The rock cycle is a continuous series of processes linking igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks; it is driven by geothermal energy (internal) and solar energy (surface) and has many parallel pathways, not one fixed route.
  • Gradualism (slow, continuous processes) explains most of the rock record; catastrophism (sudden events such as meteorite impacts) explains rare but dramatic punctuations in Earth history. Modern geology accepts both.
  • Geological processes operate at vastly different rates — from hours (volcanic eruptions) to tens of millions of years (subduction cycles) — and the rock cycle has been reworking Earth’s crust continuously for around 4 billion years.

lessons.title: Earth Structure and the Development of Plate Theory
lessons.description: Concentric Earth layers and how continental drift evolved into modern plate tectonic theory.
lessons.content_html:
Layers of the Earth

The Earth is not a uniform ball of rock. It is divided into a series of concentric layers, each with distinct properties, and understanding their structure is the foundation for understanding why plates move, why volcanoes erupt where they do, and why earthquakes occur along specific zones.

The outermost layer is the crust, which exists in two forms. Oceanic crust is dense, thin (5–10 km), and composed mainly of basalt. Continental crust is less dense, thicker (25–70 km), and composed mainly of granite. This density difference is crucial: when an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, the denser oceanic crust sinks beneath the lighter continental crust — a process called subduction.

Below the crust lies the mantle, which extends to a depth of about 2,900 km and makes up roughly 84% of the Earth’s volume. Although the mantle is solid, it is able to flow extremely slowly over geological timescales — a behaviour called solid-state flow or plasticity. The uppermost part of the mantle is rigid and, together with the crust above it, forms the lithosphere.

Beneath the lithosphere, the upper mantle becomes slightly weaker and more ductile. This zone, called the asthenosphere, is where the solid-state flow is most pronounced. The lithospheric plates effectively float on the asthenosphere, which is why they can move.

At the Earth’s centre is the core, divided into an outer liquid core and an inner solid core, both composed mainly of iron and nickel. The liquid outer core generates the Earth’s magnetic field through convection of molten iron — and that magnetic field is what makes magnetic stripes on the ocean floor possible, as you will see below.

Key Fact

From outermost to innermost: crust (solid) → mantle (solid but ductile) → outer core (liquid iron-nickel) → inner core (solid iron-nickel). The lithosphere = crust + uppermost rigid mantle. The asthenosphere is the weak upper mantle beneath the lithosphere.

Wegener and Continental Drift

In 1912, Alfred Wegener proposed the hypothesis of continental drift. He gathered several lines of evidence. The jigsaw fit of the continents — especially the complementary coastlines of South America and Africa — suggested they were once joined. Fossil distributions supported this: identical fossils of the freshwater reptile Mesosaurus were found in both South America and southern Africa, regions now separated by the Atlantic Ocean. A freshwater animal could not have crossed an open ocean, so the two landmasses must have been connected.

Wegener also noted matching geological formations: the Appalachian Mountains of North America are structurally continuous with ancient mountain belts in Scotland and Scandinavia. He further cited evidence of past climate change: glacial deposits in tropical Africa and India suggested those landmasses were once much closer to the South Pole, as part of a single giant continent he named Pangaea.

Despite this evidence, Wegener’s hypothesis was rejected by most geologists of his day. His fatal weakness was that he could not explain the mechanism — what force was powerful enough to move entire continents through the solid ocean floor? Without a credible mechanism, the scientific community remained sceptical.

The mechanism came in the 1960s. Harry Hess proposed sea-floor spreading: new oceanic crust is created at mid-ocean ridges as magma rises from the mantle and solidifies. The ocean floor is not static — it is a conveyor belt, with new crust forming at ridges and old crust being destroyed at subduction zones.

The crucial confirmation came from Vine, Matthews, and separately Morley in 1963. They showed that the ocean floor displays parallel stripes of alternately normally and reversely magnetised basalt, symmetrically arranged on either side of mid-ocean ridges. As new basalt solidifies at the ridge, iron minerals align with the Earth’s current magnetic field. When the field reverses (as it has done repeatedly throughout Earth history), the next strip of basalt records the reversed polarity. The result is a magnetic barcode on the ocean floor, identical on both sides of the ridge, that records both the spreading history and the age of the ocean floor.

Tuzo Wilson added the concept of transform faults (1965), which explained why mid-ocean ridges are offset along their length, and recognised that earthquakes focus along these offsets. The combination of Hess’s spreading model and Vine-Matthews-Morley’s magnetic evidence transformed geology: by the late 1960s, the theory of plate tectonics was accepted.

Key Fact

Magnetic stripe patterns have three essential features: they are symmetrical about the mid-ocean ridge; they run parallel to the ridge; and they alternate between normal and reversed polarity. Examiner reports flag missing any of these three features as the most common error on magnetic stripes questions.

Modern Evidence and GPS

Since plate tectonics became established, further lines of evidence have confirmed and refined it. The age of the ocean floor increases with distance from mid-ocean ridges, exactly as the spreading model predicts. Heat flow is highest at ridges (where hot magma is close to the surface) and decreases toward subduction zones. Ocean drilling has retrieved basalt cores whose magnetic signatures confirm the spreading rate calculations derived from magnetic stripes.

Today, GPS measurements directly confirm that plates are moving. The Pacific Plate moves north-west relative to the Australian Plate at about 7 cm per year — a rate that is measurable with satellite precision. GPS data also allow geologists to monitor strain accumulating along active faults, helping to assess earthquake hazard.

The driving mechanism of plate motion is described by the specification as “not yet completely understood”. Mantle convection (hot mantle rising, cooler mantle sinking) was long cited as the main driver, but current evidence weights slab pull — the sinking of dense oceanic crust at subduction zones, dragging the attached plate behind it — as the dominant force. Ridge push — the elevated position of mid-ocean ridges causing the plates to slide downhill under gravity — is a secondary driver. Students who write “convection currents alone drive plates” are oversimplifying the evidence.

The main lines of evidence are: (1) Jigsaw fit of continents (Wegener). (2) Matching fossils across now-separated continents. (3) Matching geological formations (e.g. Appalachians – Caledonides). (4) Sea-floor spreading — age of ocean floor increasing with distance from ridges (Hess). (5) Magnetic stripes — symmetric, parallel, alternating polarity (Vine, Matthews, Morley). (6) Earthquake and volcano distribution matching plate boundaries. (7) GPS measurements directly recording plate velocities today. This breadth of converging evidence from different scientific methods is what makes plate tectonics one of the most robustly supported theories in science.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Magnetic stripes questions appear regularly. Always give all three features: the pattern is symmetrical about the ridge, the stripes are parallel to the ridge, and they alternate between normal and reversed polarity. Missing any one feature costs marks. For questions on the development of plate tectonic theory, you are expected to know the sequence: Wegener’s evidence (jigsaw fit, fossils, formations) → rejection (no mechanism) → Hess (sea-floor spreading) → Vine-Matthews-Morley (magnetic stripes confirmed spreading) → GPS (direct measurement). Avoid saying convection currents “drive” plates — the spec says the mechanism is not fully understood; credit slab pull and ridge push as the main identified drivers.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Earth has four concentric layers: crust, mantle, outer core (liquid), inner core (solid). The lithosphere (crust + rigid upper mantle) floats on the weaker asthenosphere.
  • Wegener’s continental drift hypothesis was supported by jigsaw fit, fossil distributions, and matching geological formations, but was rejected because he could not explain the driving mechanism.
  • Sea-floor spreading (Hess) and magnetic stripes (Vine, Matthews, Morley) provided the mechanism and confirmation that transformed continental drift into the theory of plate tectonics; GPS now measures plate movements directly.

lessons.title: Plate Boundaries and Their Products
lessons.description: Divergent, conservative and convergent boundaries: the magmas, structures and landforms each produces.
lessons.content_html:
Three Kinds of Plate Boundary

Tectonic plates interact along their edges, and the type of interaction depends on the direction of relative plate motion. There are three fundamental boundary types: divergent plate boundaries, where plates move apart; conservative plate boundaries, where plates slide past each other; and convergent plate boundaries, where plates move toward each other. Each type produces a distinct set of geological structures, magma types, and landforms.

Key Fact

Divergent: new crust created, basaltic magma (Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift). Conservative: no crust created or destroyed, volcanic activity absent or minimal (San Andreas Fault). Convergent: crust destroyed by subduction, andesitic or granitic magma (Andes, Himalaya).

Divergent Plate Boundaries

Where two plates pull apart, tensional stress allows the lithosphere to thin and fracture. Magma from the underlying mantle rises to fill the gap, cooling to form new oceanic crust. The result is a mid-ocean ridge — an elevated submarine mountain chain running for thousands of kilometres. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge, for example, extends from the Arctic Ocean to near the tip of South Africa, separating the North American and Eurasian plates in the north and the South American and African plates in the south.

The magma produced at a divergent boundary is basaltic magma. Basaltic magma has a low silica content, low viscosity, and high temperature. It erupts relatively quietly, forming pillow lavas on the ocean floor — rounded blobs of basalt chilled rapidly by cold seawater. On land, where divergence is occurring within a continent, the same process creates a rift valley. The East African Rift, which is slowly splitting the African continent, is a present-day example.

The mid-ocean ridge system is offset along its length by transform faults — horizontal fractures that connect offset ridge segments. Earthquakes are frequent at these fractures but volcanism is absent here; the geological activity is lateral grinding, not eruption.

Conservative Plate Boundaries

At a conservative boundary, two plates slide horizontally past each other along a transform fault. No crust is created or destroyed, which is why these boundaries are called “conservative”. The relative motion generates intense shear stress, and when friction prevents the blocks from sliding smoothly, stress accumulates until it is released suddenly as an earthquake. Volcanism is largely absent.

The San Andreas Fault in California is the most studied example. Here the Pacific Plate slides north-west relative to the North American Plate at roughly 5–6 cm per year. The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake both occurred along this system. The fault is visible at the surface as a long, straight valley where the crushed fault zone erodes more rapidly than surrounding rock.

When an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, the denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate in a process called subduction. The subducting slab descends at an angle into the mantle, creating a deep trench at the surface — the deepest features on Earth. The Mariana Trench in the Pacific reaches over 11,000 m depth.

As the slab descends, it warms and releases water and other volatiles. These fluids rise into the overlying mantle wedge, lowering its melting point and causing partial melting of the mantle rock. The resulting magma is enriched in silica compared to basalt — it becomes andesitic magma, named after the Andes volcanoes. Andesitic magma is more viscous than basaltic magma and erupts more explosively. The volcanoes that form above the subduction zone are arranged in a curved line called an island arc if the overriding plate is oceanic (e.g. Japan, the Aleutians), or a volcanic mountain range on the continental margin if the overriding plate is continental (e.g. the Andes above the Nazca Plate subducting under the South American Plate).

The zone of deep earthquakes along the descending slab is called the Benioff zone. Earthquakes in this zone can occur at depths down to around 700 km, because the cold, rigid slab remains capable of brittle failure at depth. The depth of earthquake foci in the Benioff zone increases with distance from the trench, allowing geologists to infer the dip angle of the subducting slab using seismic tomography.

Continental Collision Zones

A different type of convergent boundary forms when two continental plates collide. Neither plate is dense enough to subduct, so instead the crust is crumpled and thickened into a mountain belt. This is how the Himalaya formed: the Indian part of the Indo-Australian Plate has been colliding with the Eurasian Plate for roughly 50 million years, producing the highest mountain range on Earth. The collision generates intense compressional stress, folding and thrusting the rocks into the complex structures you studied in the first lessons of this unit.

Magma at continent–continent collision zones tends toward a high silica content — granitic magma — generated by partial melting of the thick continental crust. Granitic magma is highly viscous and does not flow easily, so it typically solidifies underground as large granite batholiths rather than erupting at the surface. The large granite masses exposed in Dartmoor and the Scottish Highlands are examples of ancient magma bodies of this type.

Key Fact

Basaltic magma (low silica, low viscosity, quiet eruptions) forms at divergent boundaries. Andesitic magma (intermediate silica, moderate viscosity, explosive) forms at subduction zones. Granitic magma (high silica, high viscosity, rarely erupts) forms at continent–continent collision zones.

Seismic tomography uses the travel times of seismic waves passing through the Earth to build up 3D images of the mantle. Cold subducting slabs transmit seismic waves faster than the surrounding hot mantle, making them visible as high-velocity anomalies descending into the mantle at subduction zones. This technique has confirmed the geometry of subducting slabs and their fate in the deep mantle.

Ocean drilling recovers rock cores directly from the ocean floor. The magnetic signatures of these basalt cores confirm the spreading rate and polarity history inferred from surface magnetic surveys. Core samples also record changes in ocean chemistry and biological productivity over millions of years, providing an independent check on the plate-tectonic timeline.

Topography of the Ocean Floor

The plate tectonic system creates a characteristic pattern of ocean-floor topography. Mid-ocean ridges rise to about 2,000–3,000 m above the surrounding ocean floor. On either side of the ridge, the ocean floor deepens progressively as the crust ages, cools, and contracts — creating the flat, sediment-covered abyssal plain. At convergent boundaries, the slab descends into the deepest trenches. This systematic depth variation — ridge → abyssal plain → trench — reflects the age and thermal state of the ocean floor, exactly as predicted by sea-floor spreading.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on plate boundaries often ask you to link a named location to the correct boundary type and geological products. Practise the triplets: boundary type → named example → geological product. For the 6-mark QER, examiners expect you to name at least three pieces of evidence and explain how each supports the conclusion — not just list them. For magma type questions, the key variable is silica content: low (basaltic, divergent), intermediate (andesitic, subduction), high (granitic, continental collision). Never confuse “conservative” (plates slide past, no volcanism) with “convergent” (plates collide, subduction).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Divergent boundaries produce mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys; tensional stress; basaltic magma with low silica content and low viscosity. Example: Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
  • Conservative boundaries produce large transform faults with intense earthquake activity but no volcanism. Example: San Andreas Fault (Pacific and North American plates).
  • Convergent boundaries produce subduction zones (trenches, Benioff zones, island arcs, andesitic magma) when oceanic meets continental crust (e.g. Andes/Nazca), and mountain belts with granitic intrusions when two continental plates collide (e.g. Himalaya/Indo-Australian and Eurasian plates).

practice_questions.text:
At which plate boundary type is new oceanic crust created?
A) Conservative
B) Convergent (subduction)
C) Continent–continent collision
D) Divergent
practice_questions.marks: D) Divergent [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the zone of deep earthquakes that follows the path of a subducting plate into the mantle.
practice_questions.marks: Benioff zone [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between the geological activity at a divergent plate boundary and a conservative plate boundary.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks (2 per comparison, 1 for naming, 1 for giving both sides):
• Divergent: volcanic activity occurs (basaltic magma erupts at ridges); conservative: little or no volcanic activity [2]
• Divergent: new oceanic crust is created; conservative: no crust is created or destroyed [2]
Accept: divergent produces rift valleys / ridges; conservative produces large strike-slip faults [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how andesitic magma is produced above a subduction zone.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• The subducting oceanic plate warms and releases water/volatiles as it descends [1]
• These fluids rise into the overlying mantle wedge, lowering its melting point and causing partial melting [1]
• The resulting magma is enriched in silica compared to basalt, producing andesitic magma [1]

practice_questions.text: A mid-ocean ridge is spreading at a half-rate of 3.5 cm per year. Calculate how far apart two points on opposite plates will be after 2 million years. Express your answer in kilometres. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Full spreading rate = 2 × 3.5 = 7 cm/year. Distance = 7 cm/yr × 2,000,000 yr = 14,000,000 cm = 140 km [2 marks: 1 for doubling the half-rate, 1 for correct final answer with units]. Accept: 140 km.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the geological evidence that would allow a geologist to distinguish between an ocean–continent convergent boundary and a continent–continent collision zone. Consider the structures, magmas, and topographic features produced at each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Compares structures (trench + island arc vs mountain belt without trench), magma types (andesitic, explosive at subduction; granitic, intrusive at collision), topography (deep trench vs high plateau/mountain range), seismicity (Benioff zone deep earthquakes at subduction; shallower earthquakes at collision); gives real examples (Andes/Nazca vs Himalaya/Indo-Australian); evaluates which features are most diagnostic; reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: Correctly identifies at least three distinguishing features across the two boundary types with examples; some evaluation.
Developing: Identifies one or two differences; limited evidence; little evaluation.
Emerging: Partial understanding of one boundary type; no comparison.

glossary_terms.definition: A plate boundary where two plates move apart from each other, allowing magma to rise and create new oceanic crust.
A plate boundary where two plates move past each other horizontally with no crust created or destroyed.
A plate boundary where two plates move toward each other, resulting in subduction, mountain building, or both.
A continuous underwater mountain chain marking a divergent plate boundary where new oceanic crust is created.
Magma or lava with a low silica content (around 45–52%), characterised by low viscosity and high temperature, produced at divergent boundaries and oceanic hot spots.
An elongated lowland valley formed where tensional stress pulls the lithosphere apart and a central block drops down between parallel normal faults.
A large-scale strike-slip fault occurring at a conservative plate boundary, where two plates grind past each other horizontally.
The process by which a denser oceanic plate sinks beneath a less dense continental (or oceanic) plate at a convergent boundary.
A long, narrow, very deep depression in the ocean floor where an oceanic plate is being subducted.
The process by which only some of a rock body melts when exposed to heat or a change in pressure, producing magma that is enriched in silica relative to the source rock.
Magma or lava with an intermediate silica content (around 57–63%), characteristic of volcanic arcs at subduction zones.
A curved chain of volcanic islands formed above a subduction zone where oceanic crust is consumed beneath oceanic crust.
A zone of earthquake foci that dips steeply from an oceanic trench into the mantle, marking the path of a subducting plate.
Magma or lava with a high silica content (around 70% or more), forming granite when intrusive and rhyolite when extrusive; highly viscous and associated with the most explosive eruptions.
A technique using earthquake waves to image the internal structure of the Earth, similar to a medical CT scan.
Scientific drilling of the ocean floor to retrieve cores of basalt and sediment used to study the age and composition of the oceanic crust.
A broad, flat area of the deep ocean floor away from mid-ocean ridges and trenches, formed from old, cool oceanic crust covered by sediment.
